registers.name_in_paper: the Danish integrated database for labor market research (IDA)
registers.role: treatment (program exposure), outcomes (November employment of nurses, nursing assistants and doctors by sector), sample frame

controls and linkage (municipality of residence, marital status, number of children, age of youngest child, November address codes used to identify nursing home residence; denominator for elderly mortality rates)

registers.name_in_paper: social-benefits records / the Social Statistics Register
registers.years: 1995-2000 for leave spells; November benefit records over the sample period
registers.role: treatment (maternity and parental leave take-up, unemployment spells, leave duration)
sample frame (highest completed degree used to define doctors, nurses and nursing assistants) and new enrollment counts
outcomes (hospital stays, admission and discharge dates, diagnosis codes; AMI 30-day mortality and readmission; nursing home resident hospitalizations)

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish Register for Causes of Death
registers.role: outcomes (death date, cause of death, location of death; nursing home and total elderly mortality)

linkages: Unique identifiers allow us to link individuals between the patient register and the population registers to leverage additional demographic information.

Household characteristics (municipality of residence, marital status, number of children, age of the youngest child) are added to the IDA worker records from the population register; the age of the youngest child measures parental-leave eligibility.
Worker data are supplemented with November social-benefits records to measure pre-reform maternity leave, the new parental leave and unemployment spells.
Patient records are merged with the Danish Register for Causes of Death (death date, cause of death, location of death).
Industry information from the plant in IDA identifies hospitals and nursing homes; health workers and patients are aggregated to the county of the employer / of residence.

sample.universe: administrative data covering the entire Danish population over the period 1987-2000; health care workers (doctors, nurses, nursing assistants), acute AMI patients aged 65 and older, and elderly people aged 85 and older
sample.unit_of_observation: county x year x health care sector (hospital or nursing home) cells for the regression analysis; person-year for the take-up analysis
selection_rules: Take-up analysis: individuals who were employed in the previous year t-1 (93% of leave takers were employed in the previous year), assigned to a health care sector using the previous year's employer data.

Health worker definitions: doctors = M.D. or Ph.D. in medicine; nurses = bachelor's degree or equivalent training in nursing or midwifery (incl. specialization/advanced degrees); nursing assistants = social and health care aides or assistants with at least 14 months of theoretical and practical training.
Hospitals are observed throughout the sample period; nursing homes are only measured from 1991 onward.

Hospital quality: acute AMI patients aged 65 and older, restricted to index admissions, defined as AMI patients that did not have a diagnosed ischemic heart condition in the 365 days preceding the hospital admission (CMS readmission guidelines).
Nursing home quality: elderly people aged 85 and older (both numerator and denominator), who have a 24% chance of residing in a nursing home; location of death available from 1991.
Nursing home residents are identified from November address codes with disproportional nursing home mortalities in the population register.
Geography: 13 counties and three municipalities with county status; in the regressions 15 units (counties plus the combined Copenhagen and Frederiksberg municipalities).
sample.period: 1987-2000 (nursing homes and nursing home mortality from 1991)

construction_notes: Employment is measured as primary employment in November of each year (IDA); nurses and assistants on leave are labelled as not employed.
Program take-up parameters beta_0..beta_8 come from equation (1), estimated by age a of the youngest child on individuals employed in the previous year.

Exposure^s_c = [sum_{a=0}^{8} Eligible Employed nurses^s_{93,c}(a) * beta_a] / All Employed nurses^s_{93,c}, using the 1995 'steady-state' take-up probabilities and 1993 employment stocks; the calculation is repeated for nursing assistants.
Exposure to the parental leave reform is 3.1% on average in hospitals (2.6% to 3.6% across counties) and 1.6% on average in nursing homes (0.8% to 2.3%).

All regressions include county and year fixed effects and county-year controls X_ct (non-elderly county population, aggregate patient demographics), and are weighted by county population in 1993 (hospital outcomes by total, nursing home outcomes by elderly county population).

Standard errors are clustered at the county level following the wild bootstrap procedure of Cameron et al. (2008); 90% confidence intervals are constructed by inverting the test statistic parameter by parameter; CIs do not account for estimation error from the take-up regressions.
AMI patients are identified from ICD-8 codes 410.9 and 410.99 and ICD-10 codes I21.0-I22.9 (coding switched in 1994), following Rasmussen et al. (2011).
Unconditional one-year nursing home mortality rate = number of nursing home decedents divided by the number of living and deceased elderly people aged 85 and older, by county and year.
Cause-of-death groups (Janssen and Kunst, 2004): cancer = ICD10 C; respiratory = ICD10 J1, J4 excluding J19, J48, J49; brain = F00, F01, F03, G30, R54; circulatory = ICD10 I.
Multiple-hypothesis adjustment uses the Bonferroni correction over outcomes pooled by broader hypothesis, following Finkelstein et al. (2012).

claims.statement: The 1994 parental-leave program sharply increased the share of previously employed nurses on leave or not employed in November, concentrated among those whose youngest child is under one year old.

treatment.label: Eligibility for the 1994 parental-leave program (youngest child aged 0-8) interacted with the post-reform period

register_source.value: Age of the youngest child from the population register (FAFA, BEF, FAIN); employment from IDA (IDAN, IDAS, IDAP)

treatment.definition: A series of indicators 1(ageCH_ita) for the youngest child being of age a = 0..8 (eligibility for up to one year of absence under the program), each interacted with Post_t, an indicator for the post-reform years 1994-2000; parents whose youngest child is older than 8 are the ineligible comparison group.

timing.value: Measured in the year of the leave decision; the claim contrasts the first post-reform year 1994 with the last pre-reform year 1993

outcome.label: Share on leave or not employed in November (nurses)

register_source.value: IDA November employment records (IDAN, IDAS, IDAP) combined with November social-benefits records (SHSS) measuring maternity and parental leave and unemployment spells

definition.value: An indicator that takes the value 1 if the person is on leave or not employed in November of year t, averaged within cells defined by the age of the youngest child; the paper denotes the cell mean 'the share on leave'. Nurses and assistants on leave are technically still employed but are labelled as not employed.

timing.value: November of the respective year, among workers employed in the previous year

units.value: percentage points of the share on leave or not employed (no single coefficient is printed in the main text)

magnitude.interpretation: The share on leave rises 'from 45% in 1993 to almost 70% in 1994' for nurses with a child less than one year old; the introduction reports an increase of 15-20 percentage points for children aged 0-1.

estimand.target_population: previously employed Danish nurses who are parents of a child aged 0-8, i.e. eligible for the new parental-leave program
estimand.time_horizon: the first post-reform year, 1994, relative to the last pre-reform year, 1993
estimand.formal_query: E[Y_ita | do(program available), youngest child aged a, 1994] - E[Y_ita | do(no program), youngest child aged a, 1993]

population.description: Danish nurses who were employed in the previous year, by the age of their youngest child; pre-reform year 1993 and post-reform year 1994
subgroups_defined: nurses whose youngest child is less than one year old

identification.source_of_variation: The federally funded parental-leave program introduced on 30 June 1993 and effective 1 January 1994, which offered each parent up to one year of absence if the child is aged 8 or younger - creating an eligibility cut-off in the age of the youngest child

key_assumptions.assumption: Differences in leave-taking between eligible parents (youngest child aged 0-8) and ineligible parents between 1993 and 1994 are attributable to the introduction of the parental-leave program.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1 contrasts the age-of-youngest-child profile of the share on leave in 1993 and 1994 with 95% confidence intervals; the comparison group is parents whose youngest child is older than 8.

key_assumptions.assumption: The program does not change leave-taking among ineligible parents (no contamination of the comparison group).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper notes a slight increase in the share on leave among ineligible nursing assistants and attributes it to the education and/or sabbatical programs also introduced in 1994, judging these changes 'small compared to the increase in leave taking'; it also notes bunching for children aged 6-8.

implies_edges.from: 1994 parental-leave program
implies_edges.to: share on leave among ineligible parents (youngest child older than 8)

key_assumptions.assumption: Take-up is measured in the sample of individuals who were employed in the previous year, so the estimate conditions on prior-year employment.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 'using social-benefit-spells data for 1995-2000, we find that the large majority of leave takers (93%) were employed in the previous year'; prior-year employment also allows the sector assignment used in the difference-in-differences analysis.

implies_edges.from: sample conditioning: employed in year t-1
implies_edges.to: Share on leave or not employed in November (nurses)

threats_discussed: the educational and sabbatical leave programs introduced at the same time, which do not condition on the age of the child
bunching among parents of children aged 6-8, for whom 1994 is the last chance to use the program
pooling of male and female employees (95% of nursing assistants and 97% of nurses in the labour market are female; doctors are predominantly male)

Supplementary Table A.1 shows that parental leave accounts for 77% of total paid leave time among nurses over 1995-2000

estimator.value: OLS on equation (1), an individual-level difference-in-differences in the age of the youngest child; Figure 1 displays the underlying cell means with 95% confidence intervals

estimation.specification: equation (1): indicators for the age of the youngest child (0-8), a post-reform indicator, and their interactions beta_0-beta_8

source_table.value: Figure 1, A (top left) - Nurses; the pre/post shares and take-up magnitudes are stated in the text on pp. 2317-2318, and the full regression results are referred to Supplementary Table A.2
